Title: A hybrid framework for heart disease prediction using classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques
Author: Ankur Kumar; Sanjay Dhanka; Abhinav Sharma; Rohit Bansal; Mochammad Fahlevi; Fazla Rabby; Mohammed Aljuaid
Abstract: This research proposes a hybrid framework integrating classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques to enhance heart disease prediction. Using a combined UCI dataset and preprocessing/feature selection, the study trains and optimizes both classical and quantum-inspired SVM-based models evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.
Method Used: Classical pipeline: CGA + CPSO + CSVM. Quantum-inspired pipeline (simulated): QGA + QPSO + QSVM using Qiskit Aer simulator.
Result: Quantum-inspired model: accuracy 97.83%, sensitivity 98.96%, specificity 96.59%, F1 97.94%, AUC 97%. Classical model: accuracy 94.02%. Runtime: 413.57s (quantum) vs 362.92s (classical).
Conclusion: Quantum-inspired hybrid outperformed classical hybrid across metrics while using fewer features; higher computational cost; demonstrated via classical simulation only.
Limitations: Quantum methods on classical simulators (not real QPU); increased runtime; no external validation on larger datasets; hardware noise/coherence constraints remain.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, F1, AUC, LR+, LR-, DOR

Title: A primer for quantum computing and its applications to healthcare and biomedical research
Author: Thomas J.S. Durant; Elizabeth Knight; Brent Nelson; Sarah Dudgeon; Seung J. Lee; Dominic Walliman; Hobart P. Young; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Wade L. Schulz
Abstract: Introduces quantum computing technologies for biomedical research and highlights future applications in healthcare focusing on capabilities, benefits, limitations, and current state of hardware/software.
Method Used: Narrative literature review / primer — no original experimental model.
Result: Summarizes current quantum hardware is limited; QPUs should be viewed as accelerators complementary to CPUs/GPUs; practical quantum advantage for real-world biomedical tasks remains limited.
Conclusion: Quantum computing has promising potential for high-complexity biomedical problems but real-world advantages not yet broadly demonstrated; depends on hardware maturity and clearer benchmarking.
Limitations: Not a primary experimental study; conclusions depend on available literature; many cited applications constrained by current device scale/noise.

Title: A Quantum-Enhanced Precision Medicine Application to Support Data-Driven Clinical Decisions for the Personalized Treatment of Advanced Knee Osteoarthritis
Author: Nima Heidari; Stefano Olgiati; Davide Meloni; Mark Slevin; Ali Noorani; Federico Pirovano; Leonard Azamfirei
Abstract: QNN application to support precision data-driven clinical decisions to select personalized treatments for advanced knee osteoarthritis by classifying treatment responders vs non-responders.
Method Used: QNN (parameterized quantum circuit; Qiskit OpflowQNN); COBYLA optimizer; Aer simulator 1024 shots; train/test split 113/57.
Result: Test set (n=57): sensitivity 0.8235; specificity 0.2609; F1 0.7088; LR+ 1.1142; DOR 2.0. No information rate 0.59.
Conclusion: Preliminary validation suggests QML decision support for personalized treatment selection is promising but performance (especially specificity) is limited; requires larger datasets and clinical validation.
Limitations: Small validation dataset; low specificity/high false positives; outliers handling may affect generalizability; external validation required.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Sensitivity, Specificity, F1, LR+, LR-, DOR

Title: A quantum-optimized approach for breast cancer detection using SqueezeNet-SVM
Author: Anas Bilal; Ali Alkhathlan; Faris A. Kateb; Alishba Tahir; Muhammad Shafiq; Haixia Long
Abstract: Proposes a hybrid approach Q-BGWO-SQSVM using quantum-inspired binary Grey Wolf Optimizer with SqueezeNet and SVM to enhance breast cancer classification accuracy.
Method Used: Mammogram preprocessing + Otsu thresholding segmentation + SqueezeNet feature extraction + SVM with Q-BGWO hyperparameter optimization; 5/10/15-fold CV on MIAS, INbreast, DDSM, CBIS-DDSM.
Result: Best on CBIS-DDSM with 15-fold CV: accuracy 99%, sensitivity 98%, specificity 100%.
Conclusion: Q-BGWO-SQSVM achieves near state-of-the-art mammography classification; reliable efficient approach for early breast cancer detection; further validation recommended.
Limitations: Reliance on benchmark datasets and cross-validation; clinical real-world deployment not validated; performance depends on preprocessing/ROI selection.
Classical Baseline Quality: Unclear — compared to prior literature only

Title: A systematic review of quantum machine learning for digital health
Author: Riddhi S. Gupta; Carolyn E. Wood; Teyl Engstrom; Jason D. Pole; Sally Shrapnel
Abstract: Systematic review assessing whether QML algorithms outperform existing classical methods for clinical decisioning or health service delivery. 4915 initial records; 169 eligible; 46 high-quality; 16 with realistic operating conditions.
Method Used: Systematic review (PRISMA; SPICE; PROSPERO); searched PubMed/Embase/IEEE/Scopus/arXiv 2015-2024; quality appraisal to 46 high-quality studies.
Result: No consistent empirical performance advantage of QML over classical methods in digital health; most studies rely on ideal simulations; only 16 used realistic operating conditions.
Conclusion: Current evidence base insufficient to claim empirical quantum utility in digital health; future work must establish scalability, uncertainty, noise robustness, and stronger benchmarking.
Limitations: Many studies excluded for low technical rigor; heterogeneous metrics impede meta-analysis; limited use of EHR/real-world datasets.

Title: A unifying nonlinear probabilistic epidemic model in space and time
Author: Roberto Beneduci; Eleonora Bilotta; Pietro Pantano
Abstract: Proposes a continuous space-time nonlinear probabilistic mother model for epidemic spread based on sub-probability densities; shows how multiple deterministic and stochastic epidemic models can be derived as special cases.
Method Used: Defines infected and susceptible sub-probability densities; derives coupled integro-differential equations; under locality/symmetry assumptions derives generalized Fisher-Kolmogorov-type drift-diffusion PDE; discretizes to obtain discrete stochastic processes.
Result: Key derivations: evolution equations for infected/susceptible densities; generalized Fisher-Kolmogorov with anomalous diffusion; classical Fisher-Kolmogorov arises from linearized probabilistic model.
Conclusion: Provides a unifying probabilistic framework connecting stochastic and deterministic epidemic models; forecasting applications depend on estimating kernel W from data.
Limitations: Assumes existence and differentiability of sub-probability densities; no births/deaths in base formulation; practical use depends on solving inverse problem to estimate kernel W from data.

Title: Advancing single-cell omics and cell-based therapeutics with quantum computing
Author: Aritra Bose; Kahn Rhrissorrakrai; Filippo Utro; Laxmi Parida; Quantum for Healthcare Life Sciences Consortium
Abstract: Roadmap article discussing how quantum computing could complement AI to address computational bottlenecks in spatiotemporal single-cell and spatial omics analysis.
Method Used: Narrative roadmap/review of quantum computing analogues for key single-cell/spatial analysis tasks; no new validated model.
Result: Not reported — roadmap only.
Conclusion: Quantum computing may help overcome scaling, generalization, and sample-limited challenges in single-cell/spatial multi-omics; near-term utility depends on hardware maturity and careful benchmarking.
Limitations: Not yet clinically validated; many proposed approaches require fault-tolerant devices; major practical hurdles include data encoding overhead, noise/coherence limits, barren plateaus.

Title: An integrated strategy based on radiomics and quantum machine learning: diagnosis and clinical interpretation of pulmonary ground-glass nodules
Author: Xianzhi Huang; Fangyi Xu; Wenchao Zhu; Lin Yao; Jiahuan He; Junhao Su; Wending Zhao; Hongjie Hu
Abstract: Retrospective study developing integrated pipeline combining CT radiomics and QML (QSVC, Pegasos QSVC, QNN) with SHAP interpretability to classify pulmonary pGGNs as invasive vs non-invasive adenocarcinoma.
Method Used: CT pGGN segmentation + radiomics extraction (960 features) + Random Forest feature selection (9 features) + QML models (QSVC, Pegasos QSVC, QNN) on Qiskit noiseless simulator; SHAP interpretability.
Result: QNN: accuracy 89.23% (95% CI 81.54-95.38), sensitivity 96.55%, specificity 83.33%, AUC 0.937. QNN AUC significantly outperformed classical SVM AUC 0.833 (p=0.003).
Conclusion: Integrated radiomics + QML + SHAP improves pGGN invasiveness classification vs classical SVM; QNN performed best; supports use as non-invasive decision-support tool.
Limitations: Single-center retrospective design; relatively small sample; radiomics sensitive to scan parameters; SHAP visualization largely qualitative; scalability constrained by current quantum hardware.

Title: Applications of quantum computing in clinical care
Author: Stevan C. Fairburn; Lara Jehi; Brenton T. Bicknell; Beckley G. Wilkes; Bharat Panuganti
Abstract: Systematic review of quantum computing applications with first-order clinical relevance; summarizes evidence for impacts on diagnostics, treatment optimization, and real-time decision support.
Method Used: Systematic review across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science (Jan 2015-Jan 2024); screened 237 records; included 35 studies; thematic synthesis.
Result: QC promise across medical imaging and clinical decision-making (each 54.3% of included articles) and oncology (48.6%); many studies theoretical/simulation-based or use synthetic data.
Conclusion: Quantum computing shows potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency; clinical adoption limited by current technical, validation, and ethical constraints.
Limitations: Limited database scope; most included work theoretical/simulator-based/synthetic; heterogeneity limits generalizability; potential publication bias; lack of standardized benchmarks.

Title: Biology and medicine in the landscape of quantum advantages
Author: Benjamin A. Cordier; Nicolas P. D. Sawaya; Gian Giacomo Guerreschi; Shannon K. McWeeney
Abstract: Review proposing framework to define and classify quantum advantage and applying it across biology/medicine problems to assess where practical advantages may emerge.
Method Used: Narrative review + conceptual framework; surveys quantum algorithms and maps them to biomedical tasks; discusses practical constraints (NISQ vs FTQC).
Result: No new experimental results; quantum simulation (VQE) identified as most promising near-to-medium-term candidate; variational QML may offer potential benefits but requires further validation.
Conclusion: Quantum simulation for molecular systems is highlighted as the clearest near-term path to meaningful quantum advantage in biomedicine; variational/hybrid methods are key near-term strategy.
Limitations: No empirical data; theoretical framework only; timeline for operational advantage uncertain.

Title: Quantum-assisted federated intelligent diagnosis algorithm with variational training supported by 5G networks
Author: Arnaldo Rafael Camara Araujo; Ogobuchi Daniel Okey; Muhammad Saadi; Pablo Adasme; Renata Lopes Rosa; Demóstenes Zegarra Rodríguez
Abstract: Proposes β-QuAFIDA: a quantum-assisted federated learning framework for intelligent healthcare diagnosis via IoMT devices connected through 5G networks. Uses β-VQE optimization in a nested loop structure to preserve privacy and improve convergence.
Method Used: β-QuAFIDA: inner loop trains β-VQE to approximate expectation values; outer loop minimizes relative entropy to target. Implemented using PennyLane + PyTorch + QuEST simulator. Angle encoding. Tested on Fetal Health Dataset (2126 CTG records); 80/20 split.
Result: Central trained VQNN: test accuracy 83.90%. β-QuAFIDA (2 clients): 83.98%; (4 clients): 84.13%; (8 clients): 83.75%. Fidelity under noise: BF=0.9958, AD=0.9775, DN=0.9993. Personalized vs no personalized training: marginal gains.
Conclusion: β-QuAFIDA demonstrates robustness in noisy NISQ environments and suitable for privacy-preserving federated diagnosis; performance consistent across distributed configurations; promising for intelligent healthcare in 5G networks.
Limitations: Sensitivity to heuristic parameters R and α; tested on single dataset; no comparison to classical federated learning baselines; scalability to larger datasets not demonstrated; all quantum components simulated.
Classical Baseline Quality: No — no classical FL baseline reported

Title: IoT driven smart health monitoring for heart disease prediction using quantum kernel enhanced sardine diffusion and CNN
Author: Dibas Kumar Hembram; Satya Narayan Tripathy; CH Narsimha Reddy; Debabrata Dansana; Quadri Noorulhasan Naveed; Shafat khan; Mohammed Kareemullah; Addisu Frinjo Emma
Abstract: Proposes IoT-based Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet for real-time heart disease prediction combining quantum clustering, Q2CNN, diffusion kernel attention, and Sardine Optimization Algorithm.
Method Used: Quantum Clustering with k-Means → Z-score Min-Max Normalization → Fast Point Transformer feature extraction → Q2CNN + DKAN (Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet) with Sardine Optimization. UCI Heart Failure dataset (299 records). 70/15/15 split.
Result: Accuracy 99.97-99.98%; Precision 99.34-99.59%; Recall 98.47-99.56%; F1 96.34-99.46%; MSE 0.01; Specificity 99.27%; Training accuracy 99.9%; Execution time 0.1s.
Conclusion: Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet achieves impressive 99% accuracy enabling real-time IoT-based diagnosis; future work to integrate additional physiological parameters and address scalability.
Limitations: Extremely small dataset (299 records); no confidence intervals; quantum components simulated not real hardware; no strong classical DNN baseline; 99%+ accuracy on 299-record dataset is unreliable indicator of generalizable performance.
Classical Baseline Quality: Weak — compared to non-DNN baselines only
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, MSE, Specificity
Quantum Advantage Notes: claimed but dataset too small to establish

Title: Variational quantum classifier-based early identification and classification of chronic kidney disease using sparse autoencoder and LASSO shrinkage
Author: P. Parthasarathi; Haya Mesfer Alshahrani; K. Venkatachalam; Jaehyuk Cho
Abstract: QML-based technique for early diagnosis and prognosis of CKD using VQC with sparse autoencoder data augmentation and LASSO feature selection. Evaluated on UCI CKD dataset (400 patients, 25 attributes).
Method Used: Phase 1: Kalman filter + min-max normalization. Phase 2: Sparse autoencoder augmentation (KL divergence + L1). Phase 3: LASSO shrinkage (13 features selected). Phase 4: VQC (Qiskit RawFeatureVector + RealAmplitudes ansatz 3 layers + COBYLA + CrossEntropy loss).
Result: With LASSO: VQC accuracy 99.2%, precision 98.3%, recall 98.5%, F1 98.9%, AUC-ROC 99.1%. Without LASSO: VQC accuracy 98.2%. Outperforms SVM (92.8%), RF (90.7%), LR (93.9%), MLP (94.8%), QSVM (97.8%).
Conclusion: VQC with LASSO feature selection achieves 99.2% accuracy for CKD classification surpassing classical and quantum baselines; establishes groundwork for quantum-assisted medical AI systems.
Limitations: Quantum circuits susceptible to noise; scalability restricted by qubit/gate complexity; data encoding overhead; increased training time vs classical; tested only on UCI CKD dataset; no confidence intervals reported.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — SVM / RF / LR / MLP / QSVM compared

Title: Deep Ensemble learning and quantum machine learning approach for Alzheimer's disease detection
Author: Abebech Jenber Belay; Yelkal Mulualem Walle; Melaku Bitew Haile
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease threatening global public health. This study proposes a deep ensemble learning pipeline combining VGG16 and ResNet50 for feature extraction from ADNI MRI images combined with a 5-qubit Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) for 4-class AD stage classification (CN, EMCI, MCI, AD).
Method Used: Merge ADNI1+ADNI2 MRI images; preprocess (crop, resize 128x128, filtering, augmentation); extract and concatenate deep features via customized VGG16 and ResNet50; encode features using 5-qubit QSVM for 4-class classification; compare against classical SVM and end-to-end ensemble baselines
Result: VGGNet+ResNet+QSVM: Accuracy 99.89%, Precision 99.25%, Recall 99.23%, F1 99.13%, AUC 99.99%; VGGNet+QSVM: 95.65%; ResNet+QSVM: 91.56%; Ensemble+classical SVM: 86.78%; End-to-end Ensemble DL: 90.58%
Conclusion: Ensemble deep feature extraction combined with QSVM markedly improves 4-class AD stage classification over classical SVM and end-to-end DL baselines; suggests quantum ML can enhance classification accuracy in neurological medical imaging tasks
Limitations: Quantum hardware vs simulator not clearly specified beyond 5-qubit; uses Kaggle-derived ADNI subsets; resized 2D images may limit generalizability; single dataset limits external validation
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – classical SVM and end-to-end DL compared
Quantum Advantage Notes: outperforms classical SVM and DL baselines

Title: Clinical data classification with noisy intermediate scale quantum computers
Author: S. Moradi; C. Brandner; C. Spielvogel; D. Krajnc; S. Hillmich; R. Wille; W. Drexler; L. Papp
Abstract: This work investigates the feasibility of quantum machine learning (QML) on real clinical datasets using NISQ devices. Two QML algorithms are proposed: a quantum distance classifier (qDC) and a simplified quantum-kernel SVM (sqKSVM) using log2N linear time encoding on the 15-qubit IBMQ Melbourne device. Three open-access clinical datasets are used: Pediatric Bone Marrow Transplant (n=134), Wisconsin Breast Cancer (n=569), and Heart Failure Mortality (n=300).
Method Used: Quantum distance classifier (qDC) and simplified quantum-kernel SVM (sqKSVM); log2N linear time encoding on 15-qubit IBMQ Melbourne real QPU; 5-fold cross-validation; compared against classical SVM and KNN
Result: qDC outperforms kernel-based methods in small sample/feature datasets; sqKSVM outperforms qDC in high sample/feature datasets; log2N encoding improves AUC by up to +2% across all QML approaches
Conclusion: QML on NISQ hardware achieves comparable performance to classical methods on clinical datasets; log2N encoding is efficient for small-qubit devices; dataset size determines which QML approach is optimal
Limitations: Tested on only 3 small clinical datasets; IBMQ Melbourne now retired; hardware noise limits scalability; no large-scale clinical validation
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – classical SVM and KNN compared
Quantum Advantage Notes: mixed results; competitive but not clearly superior

Title: Drug repurposing based on a quantum-inspired method versus classical fingerprinting uncovers potential antivirals against SARS-CoV-2
Author: Jose M. Jimenez-Guardeño; Ana Maria Ortega-Prieto; Borja Menendez Moreno; Thomas J. A. Maguire; Adam Richardson; Juan Ignacio Diaz-Hernandez; Javier Diez Perez; Mark Zuckerman; Albert Mercadal Playa; Carlos Cordero Deline; Michael H. Malim; Rocio Teresa Martinez-Nunez
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the need to identify new antiviral therapeutics through drug repurposing. A Quadratic Unbounded Binary Optimization (QUBO) model is employed on a quantum-inspired device to search for compounds similar to Remdesivir from the DrugBank database. Results are compared against traditional Tanimoto fingerprint model and validated in cell culture.
Method Used: QUBO model on quantum-inspired Fujitsu device; model Remdesivir and DrugBank compounds as graphs; solve Maximum Weighted Independent Set (MWIS) problem in conflict graph; compared to Tanimoto fingerprinting; IC50 validation in cell culture against SARS-CoV-2 variants; in vitro RdRP polymerization assay
Result: QUBO predicted GS-6620 (top) and BMS-986094 (second); Tanimoto predicted GS-6620 (top) and vitamin B12 forms; all predicted compounds inhibited replication of SARS-CoV-2 variants (Alpha, Beta, Delta) and directly inhibited RdRP
Conclusion: QUBO model performs accurate drug repurposing complementary to classical Tanimoto fingerprinting; quantum-inspired screening can accelerate drug deployment for complex pharmacological problems
Limitations: Quantum-inspired not true quantum computing; limited to compounds similar to Remdesivir scaffold; cell culture models may not fully predict in vivo efficacy; Tanimoto performed comparably for smaller searches
Quantum Advantage Notes: complementary to classical; not clearly superior

Title: EEG p-adic quantum potential accurately identifies depression schizophrenia and cognitive decline
Author: Oded Shor; Amir Glik; Amit Yaniv-Rosenfeld; Avi Valevski; Abraham Weizman; Andrei Khrennikov; Felix Benninger
Abstract: No accurate diagnostic tools exist for most neuropsychiatric disorders. A quantum potential mean and variability score (qpmvs) is developed to identify neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive disorders based on routine EEG recordings using p-adic numbers, Bohmian mechanics, and dendrogram representations. Evaluated on 230 participants including depression, schizophrenia, cognitive impairment, and controls.
Method Used: EEG recordings analyzed using quantum potential framework (Bohmian mechanics); ultrametric analysis with p-adic numbers and dendrogram trees; quantum potential mean and variability score (qpmvs) computed; AUC analysis with p-values for group separation
Result: High AUC for all group separations (all p<0.0001): healthy vs schizophrenia, depression, AD, MCI; schizophrenia vs depression, AD, MCI; depression vs AD and MCI
Conclusion: The qpmvs EEG algorithm is a useful and sufficiently accurate tool for diagnosis of neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive diseases and may predict disease course and response to treatment
Limitations: Small sample sizes per group (28 depression, 42 schizophrenia, 65 cognitive impairment, 95 controls); retrospective design; p-adic quantum analogy is theoretical not physical quantum computing; requires prospective validation
Classical Baseline Quality: No – no classical ML comparator reported

Title: Enhanced cardiovascular disease prediction through self-improved Aquila optimized feature selection in quantum neural network & LSTM model
Author: Aman Darolia; Rajender Singh Chhillar; Musaed Alhussein; Surjeet Dalal; Khursheed Aurangzeb; Umesh Kumar Lilhore
Abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a pervasive cause of global mortality necessitating sophisticated prediction methodologies. This study presents a novel hybrid model for predicting CVD using self-improved Aquila optimization for optimal feature selection combined with a Quantum Neural Network and LSTM classifier evaluated on two datasets.
Method Used: Data preprocessing (missing/duplicate removal); feature extraction (central tendency, qualitative variation, dispersion, symmetrical uncertainty); self-improved Aquila optimization for feature selection; hybrid QNN+LSTM classification; algorithm to optimize LSTM weights; evaluated on two clinical CVD datasets
Result: Dataset-1: Accuracy 96.69%, Sensitivity 96.62%, Specificity 96.77%, Precision 96.03%, Recall 97.86%, F1 96.84%, MCC 96.37%, NPV 96.25%. Dataset-2: Accuracy 95.54%, Sensitivity 95.86%, Specificity 94.51%, Precision 96.03%, F1 96.94%, MCC 93.03%
Conclusion: Hybrid QNN-LSTM with Aquila feature selection accurately predicts CVD with improved precision over compared models; QNN and LSTM frameworks reveal cardiovascular risk-related physiological pathways
Limitations: Quantum components simulated not on real hardware; limited to tabular clinical datasets; no external clinical validation on independent cohorts; generalizability to diverse populations not established
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – SVM, RF, LSTM, MLP compared
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision, Recall, F1, MCC, NPV

Title: Revolutionizing heart disease prediction with quantum-enhanced machine learning
Author: S. Venkatesh Babu; P. Ramya; Jeffin Gracewell
Abstract: This study evaluates Quantum Enhanced Machine Learning (QuEML) for heart disease prediction. The Kaggle heart disease dataset (1190 samples) is used to compare QuEML performance against traditional machine learning algorithms across accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and training time.
Method Used: QuEML (quantum-enhanced ensemble approach) evaluated on Kaggle heart disease dataset (1190 samples, 53% positive/47% negative); performance compared against traditional ML algorithms; evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, and training time
Result: QuEML accuracy 0.6% higher than classical ML; training time 192.5µs faster (670µs vs 862.5µs average); positive sample prediction rate 50.03% (QuEML) vs 49.78% (classical); negative prediction rate 44.65% (QuEML) vs 44.31% (classical)
Conclusion: QuEML is a promising approach in heart disease prediction with marginal accuracy improvement and faster training time compared to traditional ML; quantum computing can complement healthcare diagnostics
Limitations: Marginal improvement (0.6% accuracy); tested only on one Kaggle dataset; quantum components not run on real QPU; limited clinical validation; does not address real-world deployment challenges
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Specificity, F1, Training time

Title: Quantum-inspired seagull optimised deep belief network approach for cardiovascular disease prediction
Author: D. Banumathy; T. Vetriselvi; K. Venkatachalam; Jaehyuk Cho
Abstract: The early detection and accurate diagnosis of cardiovascular diseases is vital to reduce global morbidity. This work proposes the quantum-inspired seagull optimization algorithm (QISOA) combined with a deep belief network (DBN) to improve identification of cardiovascular disorders. The publicly accessible Cleveland Heart Disease dataset is used for evaluation and comparison.
Method Used: Data preprocessing (cleaning, transformation, standardization); QISOA used to optimize weights and biases of DBN model; DBN for hierarchical feature learning and classification; quantum mechanics concepts enhance exploration; compared against SVM, DT, RF, MLP, FCN, PSO, GA, GWO, cuckoo search, crow search on Cleveland dataset
Result: QISOA-DBN: Accuracy 98.6%, Precision 97.6%, Recall 96.8%, F1 97.1%; outperforms all compared classical ML models and metaheuristic-based optimization models
Conclusion: QISOA-optimized DBN achieves superior cardiovascular disease prediction accuracy; quantum-inspired optimization effectively enhances DBN performance over classical and other metaheuristic baselines
Limitations: Evaluated only on Cleveland Heart Disease dataset; quantum-inspired not true quantum computing; limited generalizability to other cardiac datasets and populations; no real QPU validation
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – SVM, DT, RF, MLP, PSO, GA, GWO compared

Title: Secretary bird optimization algorithm based on quantum computing and multiple strategies improvement for KELM diabetes classification
Author: Yu Zhu; Mingxu Zhang; Qinchuan Huang; Xianbo Wu; Li Wan; Ju Huang
Abstract: The classification of chronic diseases such as diabetes remains a critical research focus. This study introduces QHSBOA-KELM: an improved Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm incorporating quantum computing-based t-distribution variations combined with Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for accurate diabetes classification prediction.
Method Used: SBOA enhanced with: particle swarm optimization search mechanism, dynamic boundary adjustments based on optimal individuals, and quantum computing-based t-distribution variations (QHSBOA); QHSBOA optimizes KELM kernel penalty C and bandwidth c; performance validated on CEC2017 benchmark; applied to diabetes datasets and compared against SBOA, PSO, and other optimization methods
Result: QHSBOA-KELM outperforms all compared models on four evaluation metrics: Accuracy (ACC), Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), sensitivity, and specificity across diabetes datasets
Conclusion: QHSBOA-KELM provides an effective method for early diagnosis and prediction of diabetes; quantum-inspired t-distribution variations improve optimizer exploration potential and convergence speed
Limitations: Quantum component is inspiration-only (t-distribution variations); no true quantum hardware used; tested on standard benchmark diabetes datasets; generalizability to diverse real-world clinical populations not assessed
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – SBOA, PSO, other optimizers compared

Title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Transfer Learning for Cardiomegaly Detection in Chest X-rays
Author: Pierre Decoodt; Tan Jun Liang; Soham Bopardikar; Hemavathi Santhanam; Alfaxad Eyembe; Begonya Garcia-Zapirain; Daniel Sierra-Sosa
Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases may benefit from quantum machine learning advances in medical imaging. Hybrid classical-quantum (CQ) transfer learning models based on pre-trained DenseNet-121 are designed to detect cardiomegaly in chest X-rays (CXRs) using parameterized quantum circuits integrated via Qiskit and PennyLane. A balanced dataset of 2436 CXRs from CheXpert is used.
Method Used: Pre-trained DenseNet-121 + parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) integrated via Qiskit and PennyLane in PyTorch; CheXpert balanced dataset (2436 posteroanterior CXRs); k-fold cross-validation; state vector simulator; normalized global effective dimension for trainability; Grad-CAM++ heatmap visualization
Result: ROC AUC up to 0.93, accuracy up to 0.87 for several CQ models rivaling classical-classical (CC) DenseNet model; Grad-CAM++ hot zone covering heart: 94% (CQ) vs 61% (CC), p<0.001
Conclusion: Hybrid CQ transfer learning rivals classical DenseNet models for cardiomegaly detection; quantum circuits may enhance clinical interpretability through better Grad-CAM++ localization; promising for health professional acceptance
Limitations: Tested only on state vector simulator; no real QPU validation; balanced dataset may not reflect real clinical distribution; limited to binary cardiomegaly classification; small quantum circuit size
Quantum Advantage Notes: rivals classical model; no clear quantum advantage in accuracy

Title: Novel Hybrid Quantum Architecture-Based Lung Cancer Detection Using Chest Radiograph and Computerized Tomography Images
Author: Jason Elroy Martis; Sannidhan M S; Balasubramani R; A. M. Mutawa; M. Murugappan
Abstract: Lung cancer is the second most common cancer worldwide presenting significant health challenges. This study proposes a hybrid framework combining deep learning with quantum computing to enhance lung cancer detection accuracy using chest radiographs (CXR) and CT images. Pre-trained DL models are used for feature extraction and quantum circuits for classification.
Method Used: Pre-trained DL models for feature extraction from CXR and CT lung cancer images; hybrid quantum layers (parameterized quantum circuits) for classification; compared against classical DL models; evaluated on lung cancer CXR and CT datasets
Result: Overall accuracy 92.12%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 90%, F1 93%, precision 92%; outperforms traditional DL methods in accuracy, speed, and scalability
Conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical approach surpasses traditional methods in lung cancer detection; quantum computing enhances processing speed and scalability; promising tool for early lung cancer screening and improved patient care
Limitations: Quantum circuits simulated not on real QPU; dataset details not fully specified; no clinical deployment validation; improvement over classical DL marginal in some metrics; scalability to large clinical datasets not yet demonstrated

Title: CODI: Enhancing machine learning-based molecular profiling through contextual out-of-distribution integration
Author: Tarek Eissa; Marinus Huber; Barbara Obermayer-Pietsch; Birgit Linkohr; Annette Peters; Frank Fleischmann; Mihaela Žigman
Abstract: Proposes CODI (Contextual Out-of-Distribution Integration), a method that generates synthetic out-of-distribution training data from experimental observations to improve robustness of ML models for molecular profiling. Evaluated on metabolomics and infrared spectroscopy datasets for phenotype prediction.
Method Used: CODI data-augmentation framework; generates synthetic OOD samples via variational autoencoders; tested with classical ML classifiers (SVM, RF, XGBoost) on molecular profiling data.
Result: CODI consistently improved classification performance across multiple molecular phenotype prediction tasks; demonstrated reduced sensitivity to batch effects and improved generalisation.
Conclusion: CODI is a broadly applicable data-augmentation strategy that enhances robustness of molecular-phenotype ML models by contextually integrating OOD information derived from experimental variation.
Limitations: Classical ML only; no quantum components; applicability depends on availability of relevant OOD reference data.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — standard ML classifiers as baselines

Title: Epidemics, the Ising-model and percolation theory: A comprehensive review focused on Covid-19
Author: I.F. Mello; L. Squillante; G.O. Gomes; A.C. Seridonio; M. de Souza
Abstract: Comprehensive review connecting SIR epidemic models with the Ising model from statistical physics and percolation theory, applied specifically to the COVID-19 outbreak. Maps epidemic parameters to physical quantities, linking the basic reproduction number R0 to percolation probability and social distancing to blocked connections.
Method Used: Analytical mapping of SIR compartmental model onto the Ising spin model and percolation theory; theoretical framework; no ML or quantum computing.
Result: Demonstrates mathematical equivalences between SIR model parameters and Ising/percolation quantities; provides new analytical tools for understanding epidemic spread and the impact of social distancing.
Conclusion: The Ising model and percolation theory provide a rigorous alternative framework for understanding COVID-19 dynamics, linking epidemic parameters to well-established condensed-matter physics concepts.
Limitations: Theoretical framework only; no empirical validation on actual COVID-19 data; no machine learning component; limited to idealised model assumptions.

Title: Error mitigation enables PET radiomic cancer characterization on quantum computers
Author: S. Moradi; Clemens Spielvogel; Denis Krajnc; C. Brandner; S. Hillmich; R. Wille; T. Traub-Weidinger; X. Li; M. Hacker; W. Drexler; L. Papp
Abstract: Investigates quantum machine learning (QML) for predicting clinical endpoints from PET radiomic features in glioma, prostate, and lung cancer. Compares QML on noisy simulators and real IBMQ hardware with and without error mitigation techniques against classical ML baselines.
Method Used: Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC); PCA feature reduction; ZZFeatureMap + RealAmplitudes ansatz; error mitigation (zero-noise extrapolation, measurement error mitigation); tested on IBMQ simulator and real hardware.
Result: QML with error mitigation on real hardware achieved competitive performance to classical ML in several PET cancer cohorts; error mitigation significantly improved real-hardware results; quantum advantage demonstrated in specific measurable conditions.
Conclusion: Error mitigation can enable clinically relevant quantum ML in PET cancer imaging; near-term QML improvements possible through circuit optimisation and error mitigation on real quantum hardware.
Limitations: Limited to classical radiomic features; dataset sizes small; quantum advantage heavily dependent on noise levels and circuit depth; hardware noise remains a fundamental constraint.

Title: Estimating China’s CO2 emissions under the influence of COVID-19 epidemic using a novel fractional multivariate nonlinear grey model
Author: Wen Lei; Shuhua Mao; Yonghong Zhang
Abstract: Proposes a novel fractional multivariate nonlinear grey model (FMNGM) to forecast China’s CO2 emissions during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Incorporates COVID-19 epidemic data and economic indicators as covariates; evaluates prediction accuracy against several classical grey model variants.
Method Used: Fractional multivariate nonlinear grey model (FMNGM); fractional order accumulation; PSO parameter optimisation; compared against GM(1,1), NGBM(1,1), and other grey models.
Result: FMNGM outperformed competing grey models in forecasting accuracy (MAPE < 2%); predicted China’s CO2 emissions trajectory from 2021 to 2025 accounting for COVID-19 impact.
Conclusion: The novel FMNGM provides better forecasting accuracy for China’s CO2 emissions with COVID-19 impact than standard grey models; epidemic data significantly affects emission trajectories.
Limitations: Grey model assumptions may not generalise globally; limited to China’s data; COVID-19 impacts are historically unique and hard to extrapolate; no deep learning benchmark.

Title: Forecasting Influenza Epidemics and Pandemics in the Age of AI and Machine Learning
Author: Oleksandr Kamyshnyi; Iryna Halabitska; Valentyn Oksenych; Iryna Kamyshna; Pavlo Petakh; Denis E. Kainov
Abstract: Systematic review of AI and machine learning approaches for forecasting influenza epidemics and pandemics, synthesising insights from historical data (1890–2025). Reviews how AI/ML methods including deep learning, LSTM, and transformer models are transforming influenza surveillance and preparedness.
Method Used: Narrative/systematic review; covers traditional statistical methods, ML (LSTM, CNN, RNN), deep learning, and emerging AI frameworks for influenza forecasting; no original model development.
Result: Reviews demonstrate that AI/ML models outperform classical statistical approaches for influenza forecasting in accuracy and timeliness; LSTM and transformer architectures particularly effective for long-range prediction.
Conclusion: AI and ML are reshaping influenza forecasting by enabling more accurate prediction of viral evolution, spread, and public health impacts; integration of multi-source data is key for future preparedness.
Limitations: Review scope may introduce selection bias; many reviewed models not clinically validated; AI models require large high-quality data; interpretability remains limited.

Title: Grading diabetic retinopathy and prostate cancer diagnostic images with deep quantum ordinal regression
Author: Santiago Toledo-Cortés; Diego H. Useche; Henning Müller; Fabio A. González
Abstract: Presents a novel deep quantum ordinal regression method combining deep learning feature extraction with quantum density matrix regression for grading medical images. Applied to diabetic retinopathy grading and prostate cancer Gleason score classification.
Method Used: Deep learning (ResNet, InceptionV3) + Quantum Measurement Regression (density matrices, random quantum features); 5-fold cross-validation on APTOS/IDRiD (diabetic retinopathy) and SICAP (prostate cancer) datasets.
Result: Competitive performance with state-of-the-art classical ordinal regression methods on both diabetic retinopathy and prostate cancer grading tasks; quantum method provides probabilistic uncertainty estimates.
Conclusion: Deep quantum ordinal regression is a viable approach for multi-grade medical image diagnosis, combining representational power of deep learning with quantum probabilistic modeling for uncertainty-aware grading.
Limitations: Quantum component runs on classical simulator only; limited dataset sizes; quantum advantage over classical alternatives not rigorously demonstrated; hybrid architecture complexity.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — classical deep ordinal regression comparators

Title: How quantum computing can enhance biomarker discovery
Author: Frederik F. Flöther; Daniel Blankenberg; Maria Demidik; Karl Jansen; Raga Krishnakumar; Rajiv Krishnakumar; Nouamane Laanait; Laxmi Parida; Carl Y. Saab; Filippo Utro
Abstract: Perspective article exploring how quantum computing could accelerate biomarker discovery across multiple disease domains. Discusses quantum algorithms for dimensionality reduction, classification, and multi-omics integration relevant to biomarker identification.
Method Used: Perspective / narrative review; discusses QSVM, VQE, QAOA, and quantum-enhanced feature selection for biomarker applications; no original experimental implementation.
Result: No quantitative experimental results; qualitative assessment of potential quantum advantages in multi-omics analysis, rare-disease biomarker identification, and personalised medicine applications.
Conclusion: Quantum computing holds significant promise for biomarker discovery especially in multi-factorial diseases and rare conditions; near-term quantum-classical hybrid approaches are the most viable pathway.
Limitations: Largely speculative; near-term hardware limitations; data-encoding overhead significant; quantum advantage over classical ML not demonstrated for practical biomarker tasks.

Title: Implementation of a Hamming distance-like genomic quantum classifier using inner products on ibmqx2 and ibmq_16_melbourne
Author: Kunal Kathuria; Aakrosh Ratan; Michael McConnell; Stefan Bekiranov
Abstract: Presents a quantum classifier based on Hamming distance-like inner products for genomic data, implemented and tested on IBM quantum hardware (ibmqx2 and ibmq_16_melbourne). Classifies individuals with disease versus controls using copy number variation (CNV) genomic attributes.
Method Used: Inner-product-based kernel quantum classifier; SWAP test for inner product estimation; binary CNV encoding; tested on ibmqx2 (5 qubits) and ibmq_16_melbourne (16 qubits) via IBM Q cloud.
Result: Classifier achieves correct classification on test cases; demonstrates proof-of-concept for genome-scale quantum classification; noise on real hardware reduces fidelity compared to simulator.
Conclusion: Quantum kernel classifiers can be implemented on near-term hardware for genomic classification tasks; O(n) gate complexity after state preparation; proof-of-concept for quantum genomic diagnostics.
Limitations: Limited to small-scale toy genomic datasets; real hardware noise significantly degrades results; scalability to full genome sizes requires error correction; no classical baseline comparison reported.

Title: Initial State Encoding via Reverse Quantum Annealing and H-Gain Features
Author: Elijah Pelofske; Georg Hahn; Hristo Djidjev
Abstract: Studies two D-Wave features — reverse annealing (RA) and h-gain (HG) — as mechanisms to encode a known initial state into quantum annealing to improve solution quality on combinatorial optimisation problems. Systematic evaluation across multiple QUBO problem instances.
Method Used: D-Wave quantum annealing; reverse annealing (RA) protocol; h-gain (HG) feature; evaluated on max-cut and other QUBO instances; compared to forward annealing baseline.
Result: RA and HG features can improve solution quality over standard forward annealing for specific problem instances; combined RA+HG provides further improvement; effect is problem- and parameter-dependent.
Conclusion: Encoding good initial states via reverse annealing and h-gain features improves D-Wave quantum annealer performance for combinatorial optimisation; hybrid classical-quantum initialisation strategies are beneficial.
Limitations: Improvement is problem-specific; no guarantee of improvement in all cases; limited to D-Wave hardware; comparisons with classical solvers limited.

Title: Medical image diagnosis based on adaptive Hybrid Quantum CNN
Author: Naim Ajlouni; Oguzhan Alagoz; Abdulkadir Karabatak; Erkan Bostanci
Abstract: Proposes an adaptive hybrid quantum-classical CNN (HQCNN) for medical image classification. Integrates parameterised quantum circuits into a CNN architecture using an adaptive SGD optimizer. Evaluates on medical imaging datasets against standard CNN baselines.
Method Used: Hybrid Quantum-Classical CNN (HQCNN); Parameterised Quantum Circuits (PQC) embedded in classical CNN layers; adaptive SGD optimiser; Qiskit simulator; tested on medical imaging datasets.
Result: HQCNN outperformed conventional CNN in classification accuracy; further performance improvements achieved with the adaptive SGD optimiser for both quantum and classical variants.
Conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical CNN with PQC layers and adaptive optimisation improves medical image classification performance over classical CNN; quantum layer provides representational benefit.
Limitations: Evaluation on simulator only; small dataset; quantum layer scalability limited by qubit count; no statistical significance testing reported.

Title: Natural quantum reservoir computing for temporal information processing
Author: Yudai Suzuki; Qi Gao; Ken C. Pradel; Kenji Yasuoka; Naoki Yamamoto
Abstract: Proposes using real superconducting quantum devices as natural quantum reservoirs, exploiting hardware noise as a computational resource for temporal information processing. Evaluates the reservoir on a benchmark NARMA time-series regression task and a practical short-term memory task.
Method Used: Natural quantum reservoir computing (NQRC) using noisy IBMQ superconducting devices; linear readout layer; NARMA regression task; 5-qubit quantum reservoir.
Result: Natural NQRC on real IBMQ hardware achieves competitive performance on NARMA-10 benchmark; hardware noise acts as a beneficial nonlinear reservoir resource compared to ideal noiseless circuits.
Conclusion: Real quantum hardware noise can serve as a computational resource for reservoir computing; natural NQRC avoids the need for engineered noise and leverages inherent decoherence beneficially.
Limitations: Performance limited by current hardware noise levels; small reservoir (5 qubits); unclear advantage over classical reservoir computing at larger scales.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — classical and ideal quantum baselines
Quantum Advantage Notes: competitive with classical RC using noise as resource

Title: Optimizing a quantum reservoir computer for time series prediction
Author: Aki Kutvonen; Keisuke Fujii; Takahiro Sagawa
Abstract: Studies a quantum reservoir computer (QRC) based on a transverse-field Ising model and investigates how memory capacity and accuracy vary with system parameters (coupling strength, input scaling, qubit count). Benchmarks on NARMA time-series and spoken-digit recognition tasks.
Method Used: Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC); transverse-field Ising model reservoir; linear readout; NARMA-2/NARMA-10 benchmarks; word error rate on spoken digit classification.
Result: QRC with optimised parameters achieves competitive NARMA performance; memory capacity scales with qubit number; demonstrates utility for both regression and classification time-series tasks.
Conclusion: Quantum reservoir computing is a promising paradigm for sequential learning; parameter optimisation (coupling/input scaling) is critical; system size directly affects memory capacity.
Limitations: Simulated system only; does not account for real hardware noise; spoken digit classification uses simplified feature extraction; limited comparison to deep learning baselines.

Title: Optimizing quantum noise-induced reservoir computing for nonlinear and chaotic time series prediction
Author: Daniel Fry; Amol Deshmukh; Samuel Yen-Chi Chen; Vladimir Rastunkov; Vanio Markov
Abstract: Advances quantum noise-induced reservoir computing (QNIRC) by using hardware noise as an expressive resource and introduces a novel circuit optimisation approach. Evaluates on nonlinear (NARMA) and chaotic (Lorenz, Mackey-Glass) time series prediction tasks.
Method Used: Quantum noise-induced reservoir computing; parameterised quantum circuits with hardware noise injection; linear readout layer; optimised via gradient-free methods; tested on NARMA, Lorenz, Mackey-Glass tasks.
Result: QNIRC with optimised circuits achieves competitive or superior performance to classical echo state networks on chaotic time-series tasks; 7-qubit reservoir; noise optimisation improves accuracy substantially.
Conclusion: Noise in quantum circuits can serve as a computational asset for reservoir computing; circuit-level noise optimisation enables effective chaotic time series prediction using near-term quantum hardware.
Limitations: Tested on idealized noise models; limited qubit count; comparison with state-of-the-art deep learning methods limited; real hardware deployment not demonstrated.

Title: Parallel quantum annealing
Author: Elijah Pelofske; Georg Hahn; Hristo N. Djidjev
Abstract: Proposes parallel quantum annealing (PQA) to exploit unused physical qubits on D-Wave chips by embedding multiple instances of a problem simultaneously. Demonstrates improved solution quality and throughput compared to standard single-embedding quantum annealing.
Method Used: D-Wave quantum annealing; parallel minor embedding of multiple QUBO instances; systematic evaluation on max-cut, graph colouring, and other NP-hard problems; comparison with standard QA and simulated annealing.
Result: PQA achieves better solution quality than single-embedding QA by averaging over multiple parallel instances; significant throughput improvement without additional hardware access time.
Conclusion: Parallel quantum annealing makes better use of available physical qubits and improves solution quality and sampling efficiency for combinatorial optimisation; recommended as default over single-instance annealing.
Limitations: Limited to small problem sizes that fit multiple instances on one chip; embedding overhead; problem-dependent scaling; not applicable to problems requiring all available qubits.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — single-instance QA and simulated annealing

Title: Performance Evaluation of Quantum-Based Machine Learning Algorithms for Cardiac Arrhythmia Classification
Author: Zeynep Ozpolat; Murat Karabatak
Abstract: Evaluates quantum-based ML algorithms (primarily QSVM) for ECG-based cardiac arrhythmia classification. Applies PCA for dimensionality reduction, converts features to qubit format, and compares QSVM against classical SVM on MIT-BIH arrhythmia database.
Method Used: QSVM (Quantum Support Vector Machine); PCA dimensionality reduction; qubit-format feature encoding; Qiskit simulator; MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database; comparison with classical SVM.
Result: Classical SVM achieved 86.96% accuracy; QSVM achieved 84.42% accuracy (slightly lower); QSVM performance was competitive but did not surpass classical SVM; both evaluated at multiple dimensionality reduction levels.
Conclusion: QSVM is a viable alternative to classical SVM for ECG arrhythmia classification but does not outperform classical approaches on this dataset; quantum methods need further refinement for clinical applicability.
Limitations: Simulation only; QSVM slightly underperforms classical SVM; limited qubit count constrains feature dimensionality; no statistical significance testing.

Title: Plasma infrared fingerprinting with machine learning enables single-measurement multi-phenotype health screening
Author: Tarek Eissa; Cristina Leonardo; Kosmas V. Kepesidis; Frank Fleischmann; Birgit Linkohr; Daniel Meyer; Viola Zoka; Markus List; Lothar Richter; Annette Peters; Mihaela Zigman
Abstract: Develops ML models using infrared spectroscopy of blood plasma to detect chronic health conditions, multimorbidities, and forecast metabolic syndrome onset. Demonstrates single-measurement screening for multiple phenotypes using a population-based cohort study.
Method Used: Infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) of blood plasma; classical ML classifiers (regularised regression, random forest); cross-validation on KORA population cohort; prospective validation sub-cohort.
Result: Detects multiple chronic conditions (diabetes, CVD, metabolic syndrome) from single IR blood plasma measurement; forecasts metabolic syndrome up to 6.5 years pre-onset; AUC > 0.7 for multiple phenotypes.
Conclusion: Infrared plasma fingerprinting with ML enables cost-effective, high-throughput multi-phenotype health screening from a single measurement; practical for population-level health monitoring.
Limitations: Classical ML only — no quantum methods; single-cohort validation; generalisability across populations/instruments needs validation.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — standard clinical tests as reference

Title: Prediction and prevention of pandemics via graphical model inference and convex programming
Author: Mikhail Krechetov; Amir Mohammad Esmaieeli Sikaroudi; Alon Efrat; Valentin Polishchuk; Michael Chertkov
Abstract: Proposes a framework combining graphical model inference and convex programming to predict COVID-19 pandemic dynamics and optimise intervention strategies. Uses probabilistic graphical models to infer transmission parameters and convex optimisation to minimise pandemic impact.
Method Used: Probabilistic graphical models (Bayesian networks); convex programming optimisation; COVID-19 transmission parameter inference; evaluated on real COVID-19 county-level US data.
Result: Framework successfully infers COVID-19 transmission parameters from observational data; convex optimisation identifies cost-effective intervention strategies (quarantine, testing allocation).
Conclusion: Graphical model inference combined with convex programming provides a principled framework for epidemic prediction and intervention optimisation; applicable to general pandemic preparedness.
Limitations: Classical approach (no quantum methods); relies on model assumptions that may not hold; intervention cost modelling simplified; data quality from early COVID-19 surveillance limited.

Title: Predictive algorithm for COVID-19 infection risk in indoor environments
Author: Chiara Rucco; Prisco Piscitelli; Antonella Longo; Ali Aghazadeh Ardebili; Alessandro Miani; Enrico Greco
Abstract: Presents a predictive algorithm for COVID-19 infection risk in indoor environments using IoT environmental monitoring data. Combines air quality measurements (CO2, temperature, humidity) with epidemiological modelling to estimate real-time infection risk.
Method Used: IoT sensor data (CO2, temperature, humidity, PM2.5); Wells-Riley infection risk model; ML-based risk scoring algorithm; real-world indoor environmental monitoring.
Result: Algorithm successfully predicts infection risk in monitored indoor spaces; real-time risk estimation from IoT data; demonstrated in office and public spaces contexts.
Conclusion: IoT-based environmental monitoring combined with predictive ML can provide actionable real-time indoor COVID-19 risk assessment; deployable as a practical public health tool.
Limitations: Classical ML only; no quantum components; limited to specific indoor environments; model assumes steady-state ventilation conditions; generalisability across building types limited.

Title: Principles of Quantum Mechanics for Artificial Intelligence in medicine: Discussion with reference to the Quantum Universal Exchange Language (Q-UEL)
Author: Barry Robson; Jim St. Clair
Abstract: Discusses how quantum mechanical principles can be applied to artificial intelligence in medicine, using the Quantum Universal Exchange Language (Q-UEL) as a framework. Proposes a theoretical basis for quantum-inspired medical informatics and knowledge representation.
Method Used: Theoretical framework; Q-UEL (Quantum Universal Exchange Language); quantum-inspired probabilistic reasoning; Pauli algebra for medical knowledge representation; no ML experiments.
Result: Theoretical framework only; demonstrates mathematical properties of Q-UEL for medical knowledge encoding; no quantitative experimental results reported.
Conclusion: Quantum mechanical principles provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for AI in medicine via Q-UEL; quantum-inspired probabilistic reasoning can improve medical knowledge representation.
Limitations: Highly theoretical; no experimental validation; clinical applicability unclear; Q-UEL adoption limited to theoretical literature.

Title: Quantum Cardiovascular Medicine: From Hype to Hope — A Critical Review of Real-World Applications
Author: Marek Tomala; Maciej Kłaczyński
Abstract: Critical narrative review assessing the current state and real-world applicability of quantum technologies in cardiovascular medicine. Evaluates quantum imaging, QML for diagnostics, quantum optimisation for drug discovery, and quantum sensors, distinguishing clinically viable advances from speculative hype.
Method Used: Narrative review using PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and arXiv; no original experimental model; assessment criteria applied to distinguish research readiness levels.
Result: Most quantum cardiovascular applications remain at proof-of-concept stage; quantum sensing (magnetocardiography) shows most near-term clinical promise; QML for ECG/imaging competitive but not yet superior to classical deep learning.
Conclusion: Quantum technologies in cardiovascular medicine are promising but largely premature for clinical use; quantum sensing is closest to translation; rigorous benchmarking against classical AI is essential.
Limitations: Narrative review susceptible to selection bias; rapidly evolving field; many theoretical claims unverified; quantum hardware limitations persist.

Title: Quantum Computing in Medicine
Author: James C. L. Chow
Abstract: Review paper providing a comprehensive account of quantum computing (QC) in medicine, covering fundamentals (qubits, superposition, entanglement), milestones in drug discovery, molecular modelling, genomics, medical diagnostics, and QML. Discusses challenges (hardware, scalability) and future directions.
Method Used: Narrative literature review; covers quantum algorithms, QML, quantum-enhanced imaging; no original experimental work.
Result: Summarises that QC shows promise in drug discovery, molecular simulation, and medical diagnostics; quantum-classical hybrid systems identified as near-term practical pathway; full fault-tolerant QC remains distant.
Conclusion: Quantum computing is a transformative paradigm for medicine but practical clinical applications require overcoming hardware limitations, noise, and scalability challenges; hybrid approaches are most near-term viable.
Limitations: Review scope only; rapidly evolving field; no experimental validation; many cited applications remain theoretical.

Title: Quantum Contagion: A Quantum-Like Approach for the Analysis of Social Contagion Dynamics with Heterogeneous Adoption Thresholds
Author: Ece C. Mutlu; Ozlem Ozmen Garibay
Abstract: Proposes a quantum-like framework for modelling social contagion dynamics where individuals have heterogeneous adoption thresholds and exhibit uncertainty during decision-making. Uses the Inverse Born Problem (IBP) to represent probabilistic social entities as complex probability amplitudes.
Method Used: Quantum-like probabilistic framework; Inverse Born Problem (IBP); density matrices for social state representation; agent-based simulation; compared against classical threshold-based contagion models.
Result: Quantum-like model better captures phase transition behaviour in social contagion spread than classical threshold models; reproduces empirical patterns of heterogeneous adoption dynamics.
Conclusion: Quantum-like formalism provides a richer probabilistic model for social contagion that accounts for individual uncertainty and heterogeneity; applicable to information diffusion and social network analysis.
Limitations: Quantum-like — no actual quantum computation; analogy may not map rigorously to quantum mechanics; model evaluated only on synthetic/simulated networks.

Title: Quantum algorithm for quicker clinical prognostic analysis: an application and experimental study using CT scan images of COVID-19 patients
Author: Kinshuk Sengupta; Praveen Ranjan Srivastava
Abstract: Establishes a quantum neural network (QNN) model for classifying COVID-19 CT scan images, comparing QML against conventional deep learning for image classification of COVID-19 vs non-COVID pneumonia.
Method Used: Quantum Neural Network (QNN) via Qiskit; CT image preprocessing; comparison with classical deep learning models; evaluated on COVID-19 CT scan dataset from India (9500+ images).
Result: QNN achieved 96.92% overall accuracy; training time 52 minutes (classical comparison also provided); QNN outperformed conventional deep learning models for specific classification tasks; faster convergence noted.
Conclusion: Quantum neural learning model for COVID-19 CT classification achieves high accuracy (96.92%) and demonstrates faster convergence than classical deep learning; QML shows promise for medical image diagnosis.
Limitations: Simulation-based study; relatively small quantum circuit; real hardware noise not addressed; convergence claims need broader validation; single-site dataset.

Title: Quantum annealing algorithms for Boolean tensor networks
Author: Elijah Pelofske; Georg Hahn; Daniel O’Malley; Hristo N. Djidjev; Boian S. Alexandrov
Abstract: Explores quantum annealing on D-Wave systems for computing Boolean tensor networks (BTNs), formulating BTN factorisation as a QUBO problem. Compares D-Wave quantum annealing against classical heuristic solvers on synthetic and real-world high-dimensional binary datasets.
Method Used: D-Wave quantum annealing; QUBO formulation of Boolean tensor network factorisation; comparison with classical simulated annealing and greedy algorithms; tested on synthetic and real tensor data.
Result: D-Wave quantum annealing finds competitive-quality BTN solutions compared to classical heuristics for small-to-medium scale problems; performance advantage diminishes for larger tensor dimensions.
Conclusion: Quantum annealing is applicable to Boolean tensor network computations and competitive with classical heuristics at small scales; BTN formulation as QUBO enables direct quantum hardware use.
Limitations: Limited to small problem sizes that fit on D-Wave chip; embedding overhead limits scalability; no rigorous quantum advantage demonstrated over best classical solvers.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — classical simulated annealing, greedy algorithms

Title: Quantum computing at the frontiers of biological sciences
Author: Prashant S. Emani; Jonathan Warrell; Alan Anticevic; Stefan Bekiranov; Michael Gandal; Michael J. McConnell; Guillermo Sapiro; Alán Aspuru-Guzik; Justin T. Baker; Mark B. Gerstein; Aram W. Harrow
Abstract: Perspective article discussing the potential of quantum computing to address scaling and complexity challenges in biological sciences, covering genomics, neuroscience, structural biology, and multi-omics integration. Identifies specific biological problems amenable to quantum speedup.
Method Used: Narrative perspective; no original experiments; reviews VQE, QAOA, quantum ML, and quantum simulation approaches for biological problems.
Result: No quantitative experimental results; qualitative assessment of quantum potential for biological sequence analysis, protein folding, neural circuit modelling, and multi-omics integration.
Conclusion: Quantum computing offers promising approaches for complex biological problems including genomics and neuroscience; near-term hybrid approaches are most viable; continued hardware progress is essential.
Limitations: Largely speculative; most applications require fault-tolerant quantum computers; data-encoding bottlenecks unresolved; no experimental validation.

Title: Quantum computing in bioinformatics: a systematic review mapping
Author: Katarzyna Nałęcz-Charkiewicz; Kamil Charkiewicz; Robert M. Nowak
Abstract: First systematic review mapping of quantum computing methods and algorithms applied to bioinformatics, providing a comprehensive overview of current state-of-the-art, future directions, and limitations. Covers sequence analysis, protein folding, phylogenetics, and drug discovery.
Method Used: Systematic review mapping; PRISMA methodology; literature review of QC bioinformatics applications; classification framework for methods; no original experiments.
Result: Identifies key quantum approaches for bioinformatics: VQE for molecular simulation, QAOA for optimisation, quantum walks for sequence analysis; most current applications remain at proof-of-concept stage.
Conclusion: Quantum computing in bioinformatics is an emerging field with active research across multiple domains; near-term hardware limitations constrain practical applications; hybrid quantum-classical approaches dominate current work.
Limitations: Systematic review limitations; field evolves rapidly; classification framework may not capture all approaches; many reviewed methods not experimentally validated.

Title: Quantum integration in swin transformer mitigates overfitting in breast cancer screening
Author: Zongyu Xie; Xiaoguang Yang; Shuni Zhang; Jingru Yang; Yun Zhu; Aoqi Zhang; Haitao Sun; Qun Dai; Lei Li; Hongde Liu; Wenlong Ming; Menghan Dou
Abstract: Proposes QEST (Quantum-Enhanced Swin Transformer), integrating variational quantum circuits (VQC) into a Swin Transformer for breast cancer screening. Demonstrates overfitting mitigation through VQC integration and evaluates on real quantum hardware in 8- and 16-qubit configurations.
Method Used: Quantum-Enhanced Swin Transformer (QEST); VQC with O(KN) parameters replacing classical O(N²) fully connected layers; tested on real IBMQ hardware (8 and 16 qubits); mammography datasets.
Result: QEST achieves performance comparable to classical Swin Transformer while requiring significantly fewer parameters (O(KN) vs O(N²)); BACC improved by 3.62%; VQC integration demonstrably mitigates overfitting.
Conclusion: Quantum-enhanced Swin Transformer with VQC layers reduces overfitting in breast cancer screening while maintaining competitive accuracy; VQC parameter efficiency is a key practical advantage.
Limitations: Evaluated on limited dataset; performance only comparable (not superior) to classical; real hardware noise impact not fully characterised; 8/16 qubit constraint limits expressibility.

Title: Quantum machine learning with differential privacy
Author: William M. Watkins; Samuel Yen-Chi Chen; Shinjae Yoo
Abstract: Develops a QML algorithm with differential privacy (DP) for privacy-preserving classification. Privacy is achieved by clipping and adding Gaussian noise to quantum circuit gradients during training. Evaluates on the MNIST classification task.
Method Used: Differentially private QML; gradient clipping + Gaussian noise injection on quantum circuit gradients; privacy budget ε analysis; variational quantum classifier; evaluated on MNIST.
Result: DP-QML achieves same classification accuracy on MNIST as classical ML with equivalent privacy budget; privacy is attained without significant loss in model accuracy; privacy-accuracy trade-off characterised.
Conclusion: Differential privacy can be incorporated into QML training with minimal accuracy loss; provides a framework for privacy-preserving quantum classification applicable to sensitive healthcare data.
Limitations: Evaluated only on MNIST (not medical data); small-scale simulation; quantum advantage over classical DP-ML not demonstrated; privacy analysis assumes specific threat model.
Quantum Advantage Notes: privacy parity with classical; no performance advantage

Title: Quantum machine learning: A comprehensive survey of models, challenges, and future directions
Author: Laiba Nadeem; Ahmed Mustafa Khokhar; Maha Fatima Shaikh; Farrukh Hasan Syed; Sumaiyah Zahid
Abstract: Comprehensive survey of QML covering QNNs, QCNNs, hybrid quantum-classical architectures, and their applications in medical AI, cryptography, and optimisation. Reviews theoretical benefits, practical limitations, and future research directions for QML.
Method Used: Structured literature review; taxonomy of QML paradigms (QNN, QCNN, hybrid); analysis of quantum speedup claims; review of applications across domains including medical AI.
Result: Survey finds QML is nascent with few rigorously demonstrated advantages over classical ML; hybrid approaches dominate practical implementations; medical AI and drug discovery identified as high-potential domains.
Conclusion: QML shows theoretical promise but practical advantages remain elusive in near-term hardware; hybrid quantum-classical models are most viable; standardised benchmarking needed for meaningful comparisons.
Limitations: Survey methodology may introduce selection bias; rapidly evolving field; many reviewed methods not empirically compared; lacks experimental contributions.

Title: Quantum neural networks with data re-uploading for urban traffic time series forecasting
Author: Nikolaos Schetakis; Paolo Bonfini; Negin Alisoltani; Konstantinos Blazakis; Symeon I. Tsintzos; Alexis Askitopoulos; Davit Aghamalyan; Panagiotis Fafoutellis; Eleni I. Vlahogianni
Abstract: Applies quantum neural networks with data re-uploading strategy to urban traffic time series forecasting. Evaluates QNN-based forecasting against classical methods (ARIMA, LSTM) on real urban traffic datasets.
Method Used: QNN with data re-uploading; 6-qubit variational quantum circuit; angle encoding with re-uploading; Qiskit simulator; evaluated on urban traffic flow datasets; compared with ARIMA and LSTM.
Result: QNN with data re-uploading achieves competitive performance with classical ARIMA and LSTM on short-horizon traffic forecasting; 6-qubit QNN; no significant quantum advantage demonstrated.
Conclusion: Data re-uploading QNNs can perform competitively with classical time series models for urban traffic forecasting; re-uploading strategy is important for expressibility in limited-qubit systems.
Limitations: Simulation only; no real hardware validation; competitive but not superior to classical LSTM; urban traffic patterns may not generalise to other domains; limited qubit count.

Title: Quantum-Inspired Heuristic Algorithm for Secure Healthcare Prediction Using Blockchain Technology
Author: Hirak Mazumdar; Chinmay Chakraborty; Satheesh Bojja Venkatakrishnan; Ajeet Kaushik; Hardik A. Gohel
Abstract: Proposes a secure healthcare prediction system combining a quantum-inspired heuristic optimisation algorithm (QKHO - Quantum-inspired Krill Herd Optimisation) with blockchain technology for data privacy. Evaluated on healthcare prediction datasets for multiple disease conditions.
Method Used: Quantum-inspired Krill Herd Optimisation (QKHO); Deep Forward Neural Network (DFNN); blockchain for data security; feature selection and hyperparameter optimisation; evaluated on healthcare datasets.
Result: QKHO-DFNN achieves improved prediction accuracy and security compared to classical KHO-DFNN and other baselines; blockchain integration ensures patient data privacy and integrity.
Conclusion: Quantum-inspired optimisation combined with blockchain provides a secure and accurate healthcare prediction framework; QKHO demonstrates improved convergence over classical KHO.
Limitations: Quantum-inspired only (no actual QPU); blockchain overhead not fully characterised; evaluated on specific datasets only; real-world clinical deployment not demonstrated.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — classical KHO-DFNN and other optimisers

Title: Quantum-Like Approaches Unveil the Intrinsic Limits of Predictability in Compartmental Models
Author: José A. Rojas-Venegas; Pablo Gallarta-Sáenz; Rafael G. Hurtado; Jesúsús Gómez-Gardeñes; David Soriano-Paños
Abstract: Extends classical deterministic compartmental epidemic models (SIR/SIS) to a quantum-like formalism using the Doi-Peliti approach, to explore intrinsic limits of epidemic predictability arising from stochastic dynamics. Quantifies irreducible uncertainty in epidemic forecasts.
Method Used: Doi-Peliti quantum field theory approach; quantum-like extension of SIR/SIS models; analytical derivation of probabilistic bounds; numerical simulations of stochastic epidemic trajectories.
Result: Demonstrates that quantum-like stochastic uncertainty in compartmental models creates intrinsic predictability limits beyond parameter estimation uncertainty; early-stage outbreak forecasts are fundamentally bounded.
Conclusion: Stochastic quantum-like formalism reveals that epidemic forecasts face intrinsic uncertainty bounds independent of data quality; this limits the practical precision of compartmental model predictions.
Limitations: Quantum-like — no actual quantum computation; abstract mathematical framework; applicability to real epidemics limited by model simplifications; needs empirical validation.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — classical deterministic SIR as baseline
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Predictability bounds, Entropy, Phase transition metrics

Title: Robust evaluation of classical and quantum machine learning under noise, imbalance, feature reduction and explainability
Author: Savita Kumari Sheoran; Vikesh Yadav; Rakesh Kumar Sheoran
Abstract: Provides a systematic comparative evaluation of classical and quantum ML algorithms (SVM, QNN, VQC, QSVM) under realistic conditions: label noise, class imbalance, feature reduction, and explainability requirements. Evaluated on multiple healthcare classification datasets.
Method Used: Comparative evaluation framework; classical (SVM, RF, LR) vs quantum (VQC, QSVM, QNN) classifiers; noise injection; SMOTE for imbalance; PCA feature reduction; SHAP explainability; Qiskit simulator.
Result: Hybrid quantum-classical pipelines outperform purely quantum models under noise and imbalance; VQC with classical preprocessing competitive with SVM; SHAP explanations compatible with quantum classifiers.
Conclusion: Hybrid pipelines merging classical robustness with quantum techniques are most effective for real-world healthcare classification; explainability tools like SHAP are compatible with QML; quantum models need noise hardening.
Limitations: Simulation only; no real hardware deployment; IBMQ/ionQ hardware evaluation as future work; dataset diversity limited; quantum models underperform classical counterparts in adversarial noise scenarios.

Title: Shallow entangled circuits for quantum time series prediction on IBM devices
Author: Mostafizur Rahaman Laskar; Richa Goel
Abstract: Investigates shallow quantum circuits with entanglement for time series prediction on IBM quantum hardware, proposing a Quantum Time Series (QTS) framework. Encodes sequential data via phase encoding and uses forward/cross-entanglement layers for temporal correlation capture.
Method Used: Quantum Time Series (QTS) framework; phase encoding with data re-uploading; forward and cross-entanglement circuit layers; tested on IBM quantum hardware; compared with LSTM and ARIMA.
Result: Phase encoding sparse entanglement provides hardware efficiency; QTS achieves competitive accuracy with classical LSTM on short-range prediction; framework scales to larger qubit systems.
Conclusion: Shallow entangled circuits with phase encoding are a hardware-efficient approach for quantum time series forecasting; entanglement structure critical for temporal pattern capture; competitive with classical LSTM.
Limitations: Real hardware noise impacts performance; limited qubit count; competitive but not superior to deep learning baselines; tested on synthetic/benchmark time series only.

Title: Studying the effect of lockdown using epidemiological modelling of COVID-19 and a quantum computational approach using the Ising spin interaction
Author: Anshuman Padhi; Sudev Pradhan; Pragna Paramita Sahoo; Bikash K. Behera; Prasanta K. Panigrahi
Abstract: Models COVID-19 spread using epidemiological SIR model and maps the epidemic to an Ising spin interaction framework solvable on quantum computers. Studies the effect of India’s national lockdown on epidemic trajectory using both classical simulation and quantum circuit implementation.
Method Used: SIR epidemiological model; Ising spin interaction quantum mapping; quantum circuit implementation on IBM Quantum (Qiskit); comparison with classical numerical SIR solution; India COVID-19 data.
Result: Quantum Ising model reproduces SIR epidemic dynamics; lockdown modelled as effective field; quantum circuit simulation consistent with classical SIR predictions; demonstrates feasibility of quantum epidemic modelling.
Conclusion: Epidemiological dynamics can be mapped to quantum Ising spin interactions and simulated on near-term quantum hardware; lockdown reduces effective coupling, lowering epidemic transmission; quantum and classical results agree.
Limitations: Proof-of-concept only; small-scale quantum simulation; no predictive advantage over classical SIR; India-specific lockdown modelling; quantum noise not addressed; limited qubit circuit.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Reproduction number R0, Epidemic curve fit

Title: Synthesizing physics and quantum machine learning for next-generation battery health prognostics: A critical review and roadmap
Author: Kian Lun Soon; Wai Leong Pang; Hui Hwang Goh; Yee Wai Sim; Swee King Phang; Hui Leng Choo; Lam Tatt Soon; Nai Shyan Lai; Chee-Onn Chow; Denesh Sooriamoorthy
Abstract: Critical review and roadmap synthesising physics-informed ML (PI-ML) and quantum ML (QML) for battery state-of-health (SOH) and remaining-useful-life (RUL) prediction. Introduces a three-generation taxonomy: data-driven ML (Gen. 1), physics-informed ML (Gen. 2), and QML (Gen. 3).
Method Used: Literature review and roadmap; classification framework for SOH/RUL prediction models (Gen. 1-3); benchmark comparison of representative classical, physics-informed, and quantum models; no original experiments.
Result: Gen. 1 (data-driven) models dominate current practice; Gen. 2 (physics-informed) improves generalisation; Gen. 3 (QML) remains speculative for battery prognostics; no clear quantum advantage demonstrated.
Conclusion: Synthesising physics-informed and quantum ML approaches represents the frontier for battery health prognostics; QML offers theoretical potential for high-dimensional SOH modelling but requires hardware maturity.
Limitations: Review scope; QML for batteries is largely theoretical; no QML experiments on real battery data reported; rapidly evolving field; practical constraints of quantum hardware not fully addressed.
